risks.risk: Macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty compressing discretionary technology spend and elongating deal cycles
risks.note: MD&A: 'The macroeconomic environment remains uncertain in the near term. Geopolitical developments, interest rate volatility, currency fluctuations, and cautious enterprise spending in key markets such as North America and Europe may influence discretionary investments, deal conversion timelines, and program ramp-ups', and management notes enterprise decision cycles remain elongated. The BRSR material-issues table names the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine region plus inflation/interest-rate uncertainty as potentially pressuring customer discretionary spending, deal cycles and business opportunities. Mitigation: transformation-led, mission-critical and regulated-industry focus; geographic risk diversification with strategic expansion into ASEAN, ANZ and India targeting a more balanced revenue distribution; a structured country risk-assessment framework covering political stability, regulatory environment, infrastructure reliability, local talent availability and currency risk; strict OFAC compliance and avoidance of prohibited jurisdictions; industry diversification into relatively stable sectors such as Healthcare, Utilities and the Public Sector.

risks.risk: Foreign-exchange exposure with a deliberately short, India-only hedging perimeter
risks.note: BRSR mitigation disclosure: Coforge follows a hedging policy reviewed periodically by an independent third party and hedges most of its net exposure in USD, GBP, EUR and AUD from India; all hedges are designated as effective, with gain or loss recognised in the revenue line, and the current policy absorbs currency-fluctuation impact on quarterly and yearly earnings. Structurally, 'The Company does not take hedges beyond a 12-month tenor, and no hedges are taken outside India' — so exposures beyond twelve months and non-India entity exposures are unhedged; balance-sheet hedging in addition to cash-flow hedging is only being 'explored'. Note a presentational change disclosed separately in the Board's Report: effective FY26 realized cash flow hedge gains/losses are reclassified from revenue to forex gain/loss within other income/expense, which sits alongside the BRSR statement that hedge gain/loss is recognised in the revenue line.

risks.risk: Concentration risk — single service line, export-dominated revenue, and North America/Europe geographic weighting
risks.note: Back-filled with provenance from the SIBLING profile/governance bundles (BRSR Section A items 16, 17 and 19): 100% of turnover comes from a single main activity, 'Computer programming, consultancy and related services' (NIC class 6201), and exports contributed 81% of total turnover of Coforge Limited during the reporting period. The MD&A names North America and Europe as the key markets where cautious enterprise spending may bite. This is a structural concentration even though the AR does not label it a risk; the stated counterweights are vertical diversification, geographic expansion into ASEAN/ANZ/India and Encora-led nearshore delivery in Latin America.

risks.risk: Cybersecurity, data privacy, model governance and responsible-AI failure in regulated, mission-critical client environments
risks.note: MD&A: 'Given the Company's presence in regulated and mission-critical environments, operational resilience, service continuity, data privacy, security, and compliance remain key priorities. The growing adoption of cloud-native, AI-enabled, and interconnected enterprise architectures requires sustained focus on cybersecurity, data protection, model governance, responsible AI, and regulatory compliance.' Managed through information security frameworks, governance controls, compliance monitoring and redundancy planning. Cyber incidents are also named in the BRSR crisis-risk row as events that could escalate into crisis situations.

risks.risk: Execution, transition and ramp-up risk in large, multi-year transformation and managed-services engagements
risks.note: MD&A: the growth model is increasingly anchored in large, multi-year transformation and managed-services engagements across travel, BFS, insurance, healthcare, retail and public sector; these 'require strong governance around transition, ramp-up, delivery performance, service continuity, and client-specific execution'. As deal size and duration rise, so does the concentration of outcome risk in a small number of programs. Mitigated through structured deal governance, leadership oversight, disciplined execution reviews, transition planning and continuous monitoring of delivery quality, productivity and service performance.

risks.risk: Talent and capability-renewal risk in AI-led engineering skills
risks.note: MD&A: 'Rapid advancements in AI, automation, data, and cloud technologies also require continuous capability renewal. Demand for specialized skills in AI-led engineering, data platforms, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and responsible AI continues to increase across the industry.' The CEO also states competitive moats are moving from scale to AI-specialist talent, making talent scarcity a direct threat to the moat. Addressed through enterprise-wide upskilling, role-based learning, platform/accelerator investment and ecosystem partnerships. Related disclosed metrics (sibling bundles): LTM attrition 10.8%; BRSR permanent-employee turnover rate 19% in FY 2025-26 (19% FY 2024-25, 21% FY 2023-24).

risks.risk: Client credit and payment-default risk, including upfront-investment engagements
risks.note: BRSR mitigation disclosure sets out an explicit credit-risk regime: due diligence before onboarding new clients including research on the customer's promoters; periodic evaluation of client financial health through quarterly filings and earnings calls; regular monitoring of client credit ratings; weekly cash-collection tracking with escalation of delayed collection patterns to senior management; regular collections updates to the Audit Committee; credit insurance 'being evaluated' for large client relationships to cover payment default and bankruptcy; and, for engagements involving upfront investments, exposure limited through termination fees or non-cancellable contractual clauses. The evaluation-stage status of credit insurance is itself the open item.

risks.risk: Climate transition and physical risk, and the compliance cost of an expanding disclosure regime
risks.note: BRSR material issue 6 (Climate Strategy and Energy Management, flagged R&O): physical risk of operational disruption at delivery centres from extreme weather, and transition risk from evolving climate regulation and disclosure mandates (IFRS S2 / TCFD, EU CSRD, SEC climate rules, India's BRSR-Core), carbon pricing mechanisms, energy price volatility, and rising client/investor expectations on decarbonisation, science-based targets (SBTi) and net-zero pathways. Financial implication is stated as both positive and negative: higher energy tariffs, carbon-related compliance costs (e.g. CBAM-style mechanisms in client geographies), transition investments and physical climate events could raise operating expenses near-to-medium term. Electricity used at office and delivery locations is stated as the most significant component of the environmental footprint and the principal driver of Scope 2 emissions.

risks.risk: Crisis and business-continuity risk across a global delivery footprint
risks.note: BRSR material issue 4 (Risk and Crisis Management): exposure to strategic, operational, financial, technology, regulatory, geopolitical and climate-related risks including cyber incidents, natural disasters, pandemics, civil unrest or supply-chain disruption; inadequate identification, monitoring or response 'could disrupt service delivery, breach client commitments and affect financial performance and stakeholder confidence', with stated financial implications of revenue impact, contractual penalties, recovery costs, regulatory exposure and reputational damage, plus indirect implications for client retention, ESG ratings and cost of capital. Managed through an ERM framework broadly aligned with ISO 31000 and COSO ERM with defined risk appetite and threshold parameters, a Business Continuity and Crisis Management framework aligned to ISO/IEC 22301 with geo-specific BCPs, DR plans and periodic drills, a Crisis Management Team, and periodic review by the Board's Risk Management Committee.

risks.risk: Workforce health, safety and mental-wellbeing risk in a high-performance technology environment
risks.note: BRSR material issue 5 (Health and Safety): although operations are predominantly office-based and considered low-hazard, inadequate practices can lead to absenteeism, disengagement, regulatory exposure (Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 and equivalent geography-specific regimes) and reputational impact, particularly around force-majeure events such as medical emergencies, pandemics or weather-related disruptions; mental health and stress-related risks are stated to further heighten materiality. Mitigations include an OHS management system aligned to ISO 45001 principles, safety drills, ergonomic assessments, fire-safety audits, incident reporting, comprehensive medical insurance, an Employee Assistance Programme and tele-counselling.

themes.title: AI-led IT services & ER&D transformation
themes.need: Q1FY27 split the bucket three ways: a soft large-cap core, a re-accelerating mid-cap tier, and an outright business-model change. TCS grew constant currency only +0.4% QoQ / +3.2% YoY despite $9.5bn of TCV (including an ~$800mn net-new SKF mega-deal), and its AI-services book annualising $2.6bn (+13.6% QoQ) saw incremental adds DECELERATE from +$125mn to +$75mn - AI is still project revenue, not annuity. WIPRO is the laggard (+0.9% YoY cc, margin -120bps to 16.0%, Q2 guided -1.5% to +0.5%). Mid-caps are outgrowing: TECHM grew +6.6% YoY cc with every vertical up and an 11th consecutive quarter of margin expansion (14.4%, +330bps); MPHASIS's pipeline is at an all-time high, 2.8x its size at the Mphasis.ai launch and +28% YoY, with AI-led deals now 70% of it (from 12%) and BFS pipeline +100% YoY, and its new Tria platform closed multiple opportunities within seven weeks of launch; FRACTAL lifted net income +92% YoY on INR 912.5cr revenue at NRR 117% with zero churn (though only +9% cc, dragged by TMT -22%); KPITTECH won $349M of new deals with 21% of pipeline now productized AI/SDV solutions. Structurally, HCLTECH is entering the AI-datacenter business with an initial investment of up to INR 3,500cr and a 50MW long-term ambition, and PERSISTENT is buying Nagarro at EUR 1.27bn EV to build a $2.9bn / 46,000-person group - European scale is now bought, not built. The new cost line is visas: TATAELXSI crossed INR 1,000cr of quarterly revenue for the first time (INR 1,021.1cr) yet EBIT fell 330bps QoQ, with 220-230bps of it onsite/subcontractor investment the CFO said cannot be passed to customers.
themes.driver: MPHASIS's guide that 'Q2 is positioned to deliver the best sequential constant currency growth we have delivered in three years' is the most falsifiable claim in the sector; then HCLTECH's AI-datacenter build, the PERSISTENT-Nagarro close, and whether TCS's AI incremental adds re-accelerate off +$75mn.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Coforge provides computer programming, consultancy and related services (100% of turnover, NIC class 6201), delivering customised software solutions, digital platforms and managed services to enterprise customers in Banking & Financial Services, Insurance, Travel, Healthcare & Life Sciences, Public Sector and Hi-Tech. Its offerings are centred on engineering, leveraging AI, cloud, data, integration and automation, delivered through proprietary platforms and accelerators plus an AI-enabled workforce including Forward Deployed Engineers in hybrid pod-based delivery units. Over the years the Company has evolved from a traditional technology services provider into a strategic transformation partner, and describes itself as the seventh-largest Indian IT services firm.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural industry realignment: enterprise demand is shifting from effort-based delivery toward engineering-led, AI-enabled value creation; the person-hour is becoming a less relevant unit of value creation.
- Three CEO-stated shifts: enterprise AI spend scaling non-linearly as clients move from pilots to enterprise-grade agentic implementations; buying behaviour shifting from headcount/capacity to outcomes (outcome-based pricing, hybrid human-agent pods); competitive moats moving from scale to AI-specialist talent and deep engineering capability as legacy delivery knowledge becomes less relevant.
- As AI adoption moves from experimentation to production, clients prioritise partners who take end-to-end ownership of systems including ongoing operation, governance and optimisation — expanding engagement scope toward long-duration, managed-services-led programs with higher value realisation over time.
- Structurally expanding managed-services opportunity as enterprises deploy agentic architectures at scale (complexity of managing models, orchestrating agents, ensuring governance and continuous optimisation).
- Management states no material legacy managed-services drag as a structural advantage versus competitors carrying large legacy run-the-business books.
- IMF: global growth estimated at 3.4% in 2025, projected to moderate to 3.1% in 2026 before recovering marginally to 3.2% in 2027; growth divergent with advanced economies measured and emerging economies stronger.
- Global inflation declined from 5.8% in 2024 to 4.1% in 2025, expected to remain contained around 4.4% in 2026 before easing to 3.7% by 2027.
- IMF World Economic Outlook (April 2026): India real GDP growth estimated at 7.1% in 2024, projected to strengthen to 7.6% in 2025, moderating to 6.5% in both 2026 and 2027 — India remains one of the fastest-growing major economies.
- Gartner (April 2026): worldwide IT spending expected to grow 13.5% in 2026 to approximately USD 6.31 trillion, driven by sustained momentum across AI infrastructure and software.
- Nasscom Annual Strategic Review 2026: Indian IT industry recorded growth of 6.1% in FY26 with total revenues exceeding USD 315 billion; Engineering R&D and BPM are key growth drivers and GCC expansion reinforces India as a global delivery hub.
- Enterprises are adopting a more disciplined, value-focused approach to technology spending — a structural shift away from discretionary spending toward outcome-driven, engineering-led transformation programs supporting cost optimisation and scalability.
- Continued expansion of Global Capability Centers by enterprises presents a structural opportunity to strengthen long-term partnerships and participate in large-scale, multi-year transformation programs.
- Margin lever stated by the CEO: programmatic use of AI to lift the efficiency of Coforge's own internal operations ('We do not just sell AI transformation. We run on it ourselves.').
- Mix lever: transition from traditional delivery to AI-powered, outcome-based constructs is expanding the addressable market and strengthening the ability to capture higher-value, recurring revenue streams across both transformation and managed-services layers.
- Encora adds deep hyperscaler relationships, AI-native engineering capabilities and the AIVA composable agentic AI platform architecture; Cigniti integration adds AI-led quality engineering that expands deal sizes and multi-tower participation, particularly in regulated and engineering-intensive industries.
- External risks flagged in the macro narrative: geopolitical developments, constrained fiscal capacity across certain economies, elevated policy uncertainty and the risk of renewed trade disruptions.
- Executable order book of USD 1.75 billion for the next twelve months as of Q4 FY26, reflecting a 16.4% year-over-year increase — described as providing strong visibility into near-term growth and reinforcing long-term revenue visibility and execution confidence.
- FY26 order intake (TCV) of USD 2.26 billion per the MD&A; the Board's Report states the total order intake (TCV) for FY 2026 reached US$2.3 billion.
- 21 large deals signed in FY26, five of them in Q4FY26 — stated by the CEO as the highest-ever number of large deal wins in Coforge's history; a growing mix of multi-year engagements.
- Robust order pipeline and a healthy large-deal pipeline entering FY27, with a steady cadence of multi-region deal closures across North America, Europe and APAC.
- Strategic win: a USD 158 million five-year engagement with a UK-based client, cited as reinforcing the ability to anchor long-term client relationships while unlocking adjacent revenue streams over the contract lifecycle.
- Increasing velocity and median size of the large contracts signed during the year, attributed to investment in sales and marketing despite challenging market conditions.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Coforge is an asset-light IT/ITeS business and the annual report discloses no plants, no installed capacity and no rupee capex programme; its 'expansion' is inorganic, footprint- and platform-led. INORGANIC: (a) Encora — acquired via a share-swap under the SSPA dated December 26, 2025; on completion (April 23, 2026, post year-end) the Company allotted 9,37,96,508 equity shares of FV INR 2 at INR 1,815.91 per share, and Encora adds nearshore delivery capability particularly in Latin America, deep hyperscaler relationships, AI-native engineering capability and the AIVA composable agentic AI platform architecture, plus access to new client segments and specialised engineering talent pools. (b) Cigniti Technologies — the Scheme of Amalgamation of Cigniti with and into Coforge (Board approval December 27, 2024; NCLT court-convened meetings December 06, 2025 chaired by Mr. L. N. Gupta (IAS) (Retd.); NCLT Chandigarh order dated April 29, 2026) has become effective with appointed date April 01, 2025; the transferor stands amalgamated and dissolved without winding up, share exchange ratio 1:1 (one INR 2 share of Coforge for every one INR 10 share of Cigniti), record date fixed May 16, 2026. The Scheme was intended to enhance operational integration, streamline the corporate structure, eliminate duplicate workstreams and administrative overheads, reduce operating costs, enable market expansion and cross-selling, and pool technological resources and talent. FUNDING / CAPITAL STRUCTURE: authorised share capital was increased from INR 77,00,00,000 (38,50,00,000 equity shares of INR 2) to INR 1,02,00,00,000 (51,00,00,000 equity shares of INR 2) by creating 12,50,00,000 additional INR 2 shares, with consequent alteration of Clause V of the MoA (Board and shareholders, December 26, 2025 / postal ballot concluded January 25, 2026); Section 186 limits were increased for (i) acquiring the Target Companies' shares for a consideration of INR 1,70,32,60,16,842 and (ii) providing guarantees for a bridge loan of up to USD 550 mn in an overseas subsidiary if required; a QIP of up to USD 550 mn was authorised but, after the Encora acquisition completed on April 23, 2026, the Company did NOT proceed with the QIP and instead secured a USD 550 million three-year term loan facility at a fixed interest rate of 4.6% per annum from a consortium of international lenders to retire the debt in Encora — the QIP resolution remains valid but the Company does not currently intend to utilise it. ORGANIC / CAPABILITY BUILD-OUT: targeted investments to strengthen future readiness across digital engineering, cloud-native architectures, AI-ready data platforms and AI infrastructure, with increased investment in AI computes, multi-model ecosystems and enterprise-grade platforms; deliberate investment in owned compute, multi-model architectures, sovereign AI infrastructure and hyperscaler partnerships; a portfolio of more than 50 AI accelerators and 300+ enterprise AI deployments; geographic expansion focused on North America, Europe and emerging nearshore locations. DELIVERY FOOTPRINT (back-filled with provenance from the SIBLING profile bundle, BRSR Section A 'Details of the listed entity', Q18/Q19): Number of Plants stated as 'NA' for both National and International; 12 national offices and 20 international offices, footnoted as 'Delivery centers', total 32; markets served span 19 Indian states and 26 countries including India (the count includes virtual offices, sales offices and delivery centers). BRSR Principle 2 Essential Indicator 1 states that capex investments in specific technologies to improve environmental and social impacts were Nil (a stated nil) in both FY 2025-26 and FY 2024-25, while the corresponding R&D percentage was 3% in FY 2025-26 (Nil in FY 2024-25), described as 'Investments made in developing new products and platforms' — these are percentages of total R&D/capex, not rupee quanta.
